description_full: Nordic American Tankers Limited, a tanker company, owns, operates, and charters double-hull tankers in Bermuda and internationally. As of December 31, 2025, the company fleet consisted of 20 Suezmax crude oil tankers. It serves oil companies, oil traders, and other entities requiring crude oil transportation services. The company was formerly known as Nordic American Tanker Shipping Limited and changed its name to American Tankers Limited in June, 2011. The company was incorporated in 1995 and is based in Hamilton, Bermuda.

culture_narrative: Employs approximately 18 people. Revenue per employee of $16.2M ranks in the top quartile among Energy peers, improving at 61%/yr — growing workforce leverage. Each employee generates $1.1M of free cash flow annually.
financial_summary: Nordic American Tankers Limited is a small-cap energy business with a $1.4B market cap on $292M of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at -5% over the past three years, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome. Operating margins are expanding by +41.8pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 6% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $20M in free cash flow — roughly 7 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.62× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 3.6× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and thin 1.3× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.
Management returns a meaningful 6.0% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 5.7% of the shares.

sect: Its 16% operating margin is roughly in line with the Energy median (16%).
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.46x).
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-42.9% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.05 across 202 companies in the universe; the top four hold 40% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 156% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 25% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 42% and a beta of 0.68, it is more defensive than the market.
About $33.2M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 51% in the 2020 crash, 35% in the 2022 bear market and 38% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $5.85 (margin of safety -14%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 84%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $4.20 to $8.21 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Energy peers: EV/EBITDA 10.1 vs 6.9 and P/FCF 71.2 vs 14.3 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 187% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 1.4% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 2.8% (vs the 8% bar).
The 2 covering analysts target $8.50 on average, 27% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 6% falls short of the cost of capital of 8.7%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 16.58).
It converts 7% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.62x.
ROE of 3% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.0x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 13pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 3.6x net debt to EBITDA ($45.9M of cash against $424.1M of debt), and interest cover is thin at 1.3x.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -4.9% over 3 years and -3.8% over 5 years.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded -29.1% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs only 0.0x depreciation (0.0% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
own: Insiders own 5.7%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 58%.
It returns 6.0% a year to shareholders (16.2% in dividends).
The share count has grown 6.9% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It pays out 105% of earnings, more than it earns, so the dividend is at risk.
people: With about 18 employees, each generates about $16.2M of revenue, 8.0x the Energy median, and productivity has risen 61.5% a year.
That works out to $1.1M of free cash flow per employee.
The company is founder-led, which often keeps management aligned with long-term owners.
